The EASIN Catalogue

Source: vignettes/easin-catalogue.Rmd
easin-catalogue.Rmd

Introduction

Load reasin with:

library(reasin)

To retrieve species data from the EASIN Catalogue Web Service you need to use the function get_species(). Behind the screen several API endpoints will be called, depending on the arguments used. In this article we show what you can do with get_species().

Overview of all species

The first, basic way to get species data is to call get_species() without any arguments. This will retrieve all species from the EASIN Catalogue:

get_species()

You can limit the number of rows returned by using the limit argument. For example, to get only the first 10 species:

get_species(limit = 10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 12
#>    EasinID Name     Authorship LSID  Reference HasImpact IsEUConcern IsMSConcern
#>    <chr>   <chr>    <chr>      <chr> <chr>     <lgl>     <lgl>       <lgl>      
#>  1 R19422  Candida… "Fagen et… urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  2 R11525  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  3 R19423  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  4 R19424  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  5 R19425  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  6 R19426  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  7 R19427  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  8 R19428  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#>  9 R11526  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… TRUE      FALSE       FALSE      
#> 10 R19429  Candida… ""         urn:… https://… FALSE     FALSE       FALSE      
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: IsOutermostConcern <lgl>, IsPartNative <lgl>,
#> #   IsHorizonScanning <lgl>, Status <chr>

Aside the EASIN_ID and columns containing scientific name (Name and Authorship), the returned data frame contains columns important for understanding the species distribution and status in Europe, such as HasImpact, IsEUConcern and IsMSConcern (is a taxon of concern for some Member States?), IsPartNative (is the taxon native for at least one Member State?). However, if you want to know more about for example its taxonomy, the native range, the pathways of introduction and the environments it inhabits, you need to use get_species() with specific arguments. So, read on!

Detailed information for some species

Information by easin_id

The most straightforward way to get species information is to provide one or more EASIN IDs via the easin_id argument:

some_species <- get_species(easin_id = c("R00460", "R12250"))
some_species
#> # A tibble: 2 × 27
#>   EASINID Name       Authorship FirstIntroductionsInEU PresentInCountries Status
#>   <chr>   <chr>      <chr>      <list>                 <list>             <chr> 
#> 1 R00460  Ailanthus… (Mill.) S… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [54 × 1]>      A     
#> 2 R12250  Procambar… (Girard, … <df [1 × 3]>           <df [24 × 1]>      A     
#> # ℹ 21 more variables: HasImpact <lgl>, IsEUConcern <lgl>, EUConcernName <lgl>,
#> #   IsOutermostConcern <lgl>, ConcernedOutermostRegions <list>,
#> #   IsMSConcern <lgl>, ConcernedMS <lgl>, IsPartNative <lgl>,
#> #   NativeRange <lgl>, IsHorizonScanning <lgl>, LastRevisionDate <lgl>,
#> #   Kingdom <chr>, Phylum <chr>, Class <chr>, Order <chr>, Family <chr>,
#> #   ImpactSources <list>, ImpactOnSectors <list>, CommonNames <list>,
#> #   Synonyms <list>, CBD_Pathways <list>

Information by scientific name or taxonomy

You can also get species by their scientific name (or part of it) using the scientific_name argument. For example, to get all species whose scientific name contains "Aceria ambrosia" or "Procambarus":

get_species(scientific_name = c("Aceria ambrosia", "Procambarus"))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 27
#>   EASINID Name       Authorship FirstIntroductionsInEU PresentInCountries Status
#>   <chr>   <chr>      <chr>      <list>                 <list>             <chr> 
#> 1 R16888  Aceria am… Wilson, 1… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [1 × 1]>       A     
#> 2 R12248  Procambar… Girard, 1… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [1 × 1]>       A     
#> 3 R12250  Procambar… (Girard, … <df [1 × 3]>           <df [24 × 1]>      A     
#> 4 R17660  Procambar… Lyko, 2017 <df [1 × 3]>           <df [17 × 1]>      A     
#> # ℹ 21 more variables: HasImpact <lgl>, IsEUConcern <lgl>, EUConcernName <chr>,
#> #   IsOutermostConcern <lgl>, ConcernedOutermostRegions <list>,
#> #   IsMSConcern <lgl>, ConcernedMS <lgl>, IsPartNative <lgl>,
#> #   NativeRange <lgl>, IsHorizonScanning <lgl>, LastRevisionDate <lgl>,
#> #   Kingdom <chr>, Phylum <chr>, Class <chr>, Order <chr>, Family <chr>,
#> #   ImpactSources <list>, ImpactOnSectors <list>, CommonNames <list>,
#> #   Synonyms <list>, CBD_Pathways <list>

Or you can use taxon and provide a character named vector with the taxon name(s) named by their taxonomic rank(s):

get_species(taxon = c(order = "Cumacea", family = "Varunidae"))
#> # A tibble: 11 × 27
#>    EASINID Name      Authorship FirstIntroductionsInEU PresentInCountries Status

#> #   IsOutermostConcern <lgl>, ConcernedOutermostRegions <list>,
#> #   IsMSConcern <lgl>, ConcernedMS <list>, IsPartNative <lgl>,
#> #   NativeRange <list>, IsHorizonScanning <lgl>, LastRevisionDate <lgl>,

Use ranks() to look up all the ranks you can use:

ranks()
#> # A tibble: 5 × 1
#>   rank   
#>   <chr>  
#> 1 kingdom
#> 2 phylum 
#> 3 class  
#> 4 order  
#> 5 family

Information by countries or regions

There are some arguments you can use to get detailed information at country/regional level:

  • present_in_country: to get species present in one or more countries, probably one of the most useful arguments.
  • native_in_country: to get species native in one or more countries.
  • country_code: to get species of Member State concern for one or more countries. Very few Member States have communicated this information to the European Commission, so it could be that you get an empty data frame back.
  • region_code: to get species of outermost regions concern for one or more regions.

You must use ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes. Still, you don’t have to remember all the country codes: you can use the countries() function to get a data frame with all country codes and their description:

countries()
#> # A tibble: 28 × 2
#>    country  country_code
#>    <chr>    <chr>       
#>  1 Austria  AT          
#>  2 Belgium  BE          
#>  3 Bulgaria BG          
#>  4 Croatia  HR          
#>  5 Cyprus   CY          
#>  6 Czechia  CZ          
#>  7 Denmark  DK          
#>  8 Estonia  EE          
#>  9 Finland  FI          
#> 10 France   FR          
#> # ℹ 18 more rows

Similar for outermost regions, you can use the regions() function to get the codes and their description:

regions()
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   region         region_code
#>   <chr>          <chr>      
#> 1 Canary Islands ES7        
#> 2 Guadeloupe     FRY1       
#> 3 Martinique     FRY2       
#> 4 French Guiana  FRY3       
#> 5 Reunion        FRY4       
#> 6 Mayotte        FRY5       
#> 7 Saint Martin   FRY6       
#> 8 Azores         PT2        
#> 9 Madeira        PT3

Information by environment, impact or status

You can also get species by the environments they inhabit. For example, to get all species inhabiting freshwater environments:

freshwater_species <- get_species(environment = "FRW")
head(freshwater_species)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 27
#>   EASINID Name       Authorship FirstIntroductionsInEU PresentInCountries Status
#>   <chr>   <chr>      <chr>      <list>                 <list>             <chr> 
#> 1 R00024  Abramis b… (Linnaeus… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [33 × 1]>      A     
#> 2 R00070  Acanthoce… (Müller, … <df [1 × 3]>           <df [1 × 1]>       C     
#> 3 R00094  Acanthuru… Steindach… <NULL>                 <df [10 × 1]>      A     
#> 4 R00174  Acipenser… Brandt, 1… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [21 × 1]>      A     
#> 5 R00176  Acipenser… Brandt & … <df [1 × 3]>           <df [14 × 1]>      A     
#> 6 R00179  Acipenser… Linnaeus,… <df [1 × 3]>           <df [20 × 1]>      A     
#> # ℹ 21 more variables: HasImpact <lgl>, IsEUConcern <lgl>, EUConcernName <chr>,
#> #   IsOutermostConcern <lgl>, ConcernedOutermostRegions <list>,
#> #   IsMSConcern <lgl>, ConcernedMS <list>, IsPartNative <lgl>,
#> #   NativeRange <list>, IsHorizonScanning <lgl>, LastRevisionDate <lgl>,
#> #   Kingdom <chr>, Phylum <chr>, Class <chr>, Order <chr>, Family <chr>,
#> #   ImpactSources <list>, ImpactOnSectors <list>, CommonNames <list>,
#> #   Synonyms <list>, CBD_Pathways <list>

How to remember all the environment codes? Not easy, right? Don’t worry: you can use the environments() function to get a data frame with all environment codes and their description:

environments()
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   environment env_code
#>   <chr>       <chr>   
#> 1 marine      MAR     
#> 2 freshwater  FRW     
#> 3 terrestrial TER     
#> 4 oligohaline OLI

Similar to environments, you can use the impacts() and statuses() functions to get the codes and their description related to impact and status:

statuses()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   status       status_code
#>   <chr>        <chr>      
#> 1 Alien        A          
#> 2 Cryptogenic  C          
#> 3 Questionable Q
impacts()
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   impact impact_code
#>   <chr>  <chr>      
#> 1 high   hi         
#> 2 low    lo

Information by general criteria

There also are other arguments you can use to get species by more general criteria:

  • union_concern: to get species of Union concern. Only TRUE is allowed.
  • horizon: to get species coming from Horizon Scanning assessments. Only TRUE is allowed.
  • partly_native: to get species which are native in one or more EU countries. Only TRUE is allowed.

For example, to get all species of Union concern:

get_species(union_concern = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 114 × 27
#>    EASINID Name      Authorship FirstIntroductionsInEU PresentInCountries Status
#>    <chr>   <chr>     <chr>      <list>                 <list>             <chr> 
#>  1 R00046  Acacia m… De Wild.   <df [1 × 3]>           <df [8 × 1]>       A
